{{For|the asteroid|10831 Takamagahara}}{{Jmyth infobox}}{{short description|Japanese mythological place}} In [[Japanese mythology]], {{nihongo|'''Takamagahara'''|高天原||"Plane of High [[:en:Heaven|Heaven]]" or "High Plane of Heaven"}}, also read as '''Takaamanohara''', '''Takamanohara''', '''Takaamagahara''', or '''Takaamahara''', is the abode of the heavenly gods (''[[amatsukami]]''). Often depicted as located up in the sky, it is believed to be connected to the Earth by the bridge ''[[Ame-no-ukihashi]]'' (the "Floating Bridge of Heaven").
== Overview == In [[Shinto]], ''ame'' ([[:en:Heaven|Heaven]]) is a lofty, sacred world, the home of the ''[[Kotoamatsukami]]''. Some scholars have attempted to explain the myth of descent of the gods from the Takamagahara as an allegory of the migration of peoples. However, it is likely to have referred from the beginning to a higher world in a religious sense. A Shinto myth explains that at the time of [[:en:Creation myth|creation]], light, pure elements branched off to become heaven (''[[:en:天|ame]]''). Heavy, turbid elements branched off to become earth (''[[:en:地|tsuchi]]''). ''Ame'' became the home of the ''amatsukami'' or gods of heaven, while ''tsuchi'' became the home of ''[[kunitsukami]]'' or gods of the land. The ''amatsukami'' are said to have descended from heaven to pacify and perfect this world.<ref>Basic Terms of Shinto'', Kokugakuin University, Tokyo 1985 p. 2.</ref>
== According to the ''Kojiki'' == In the beginning of the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (Records of Ancient Matters), Takamagahara is mentioned as the birthplace of the gods.<ref name="Ishibashi 182">{{Cite journal|last1=Ishibashi|first1=T. |last2=Dumoulin|first2=H.|date=January 1940|title=Yuiitsu-Shinto Myobo-Yoshu. Lehrabriss des Yuiitsu-Shinto|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=3|issue=1|pages=182|doi=10.2307/2382411 |jstor=2382411|issn=0027-0741}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Chaudhuri|first=Saroj Kumar |title=Hindu gods and goddesses in Japan|date=2003|publisher=Vedams eBooks (P) Ltd|isbn=81-7936-009-1 |location=New Delhi|oclc=54072517}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Stefan|last2=Brownlee |first2=John S.|last3=Mehl |first3=Margaret|date=1999 |title=Japanese Historians and the National Myths, 1600-1945: The Age of the Gods and Emperor Jinmu|journal=Journal of Japanese Studies|volume=25|issue=2|pages=406|doi=10.2307/133327 |jstor=133327|issn=0095-6848}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Matsunaga |first=Alicia Orloff|date=1966|title=The Land of Natural Affirmation. Pre-Buddhist Japan |journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=21|issue=1/2 |pages=203–209 |doi=10.2307/2383411 |jstor=2383411|issn=0027-0741}}</ref> It is assumed that Takamagahara existed in clouds above sea because there is a scene in which [[Kuniumi]] (国生み), the god of islands, lowers his spear to form an island. Also, when the goddess of the sun, [[Amaterasu]] (天照大御神) was born, she was commanded to rule Takamagahara by [[Izanagi]] (伊弉諾), the creator deity of creation and life.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|date=2006-04-01 |title=Nanzan guide to Japanese religions}}</ref><ref name="hdl.handle.net">{{Cite journal|title=天孫降臨説話と中臣・藤原氏 {{!}} 九大コレクション {{!}} 九州大学附属図書館|year=1971 |volume=103 |url=http://hdl.handle.net/2324/2236684 |language=ja |doi=10.15017/2236684|hdl=2324/2236684|last1=田村 |first1=圓澄 |journal=史淵 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=国生み {{!}} 神社本庁 |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/shinto/shinwa/story1|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.jinjahoncho.or.jp}}</ref> In the part related to [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] (スサノヲ, the brother of Amaterasu), Takamagahara is described as the place where many gods live with Ama-no-yasukawa (天の安河), Ama-no-iwato (天岩戸), paddy fields, and a place for weaving, giving an impression that life was close to the human world.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kirkland|first=Russell|title=Taoist Political Thought |journal=Encyclopedia of Political Theory|year=2010 |location=Thousand Oaks, CA |publisher=SAGE Publications, Inc.|doi=10.4135/9781412958660.n442|isbn=978-1-4129-5865-3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author=Sheets, William J. |year=2017 |title=Mythology in 21st Century Japan: A Study of Ame no Uzume no Mikoto|journal=OhioLINK}}</ref> It is stated that the [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]] (葦原の中つ国, the world between Heaven and Hell) was subjugated by the gods from Takamagahara, and the grandson of Amaterasu, [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] (瓊瓊杵尊), descended from Takamagahara to rule the area. From then on, the emperor, a descendant of Ninigi-no-Mikoto owned Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hardacre|first=Helen |title=Shinto: a history |year=2017|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1 |location=New York|publisher=Oxford University Press |oclc=947145263}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Isomae |first=Jun'ichi |date=2000-05-01 |title=Reappropriating the Japanese Myths: Motoori Norinaga and the Creation Myths of the Kojiki and Nihon shoki |journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|doi=10.18874/jjrs.27.1-2.2000.15-39 |issn=0304-1042|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[File:Origin_of_Iwato_Kagura_Dance_Amaterasu_by_Toyokuni_III_(Kunisada)_1856.png|thumb|Amaterasu, the Goddess of the [[sun]] and the universe.]] [[File:Kojiki Shinpukuji.jpg|thumb|A page from the Shinpukuji manuscript of the ''Kojiki'']]
== According to the other chronicles == In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' (日本書紀, ''The Chronicles of Japan''), there is almost no mention of Takamagahara in the text. It appears only in the fourth book of the first stage of {{nihongo3||神代記|Jindaiki}} and part of the [[:en:Posthumous name|Posthumous name]] which was given to [[:en:Empress Jitō|Empress Jito]] in the fourth year of [[Yōrō|Yoro era]] (720).<ref name="hdl.handle.net"/><ref name=":1"/><ref>{{Cite book |title=Imagining Exile in Heian Japan|date=2017-12-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-5497-3 |pages=17–42|doi=10.1515/9780824854973-003}}</ref>
In contrast, in the ''[[Fudoki]]'' (風土記, ancient reports on provincial culture and [[:en:Oral tradition|Oral tradition]]) written in [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] (710–794), the word Takamagahara appears only at the beginning of [[:ja:常陸国風土記|Hitachi-no-Kuni-Fudoki]] (常陸の国風土記).<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" />
Similarly, in the main text of ''[[Kogo Shūi|Kogo Shui]]'' (古語拾遺), a historical record written in the early [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (794–1185), Takamagahara is mentioned only in the section of Ninigi-no-Mikoto.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Naumann|first=Nelly|date=1982 |title="Sakahagi": The "Reverse Flaying" of the Heavenly Piebald Horse|journal=Asian Folklore Studies|volume=41|issue=1|pages=7–38 |doi=10.2307/1178306|jstor=1178306 |issn=0385-2342}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kanetomo|first=Yoshida|date=1992|title=Yuiitsu Shinto Myobo Yoshu|journal=Monumenta Nipponica |volume=47|issue=2 |pages=137–161|doi=10.2307/2385235|jstor=2385235|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
In modern times, Takamagahara was described as the "supreme celestial sphere" (至美天球) in ''Tales of the Spirit World'' ([[:ja:霊界物語|霊界物語]]) by [[:en:Onisaburo Deguchi|Onisaburo Deguchi]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Prophet Motive|date=2017-12-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0 |pages=20–44|doi=10.1515/9780824864040-003}}</ref> The "supreme celestial sphere" is illustrated as a spiritual world of pure light in the radiant universe.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Young|first=Richard Fox|date=1989|title=The Little-Lad Deity and the Dragon Princess. Jesus in a New World-Renewal Movement|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=44|issue=1|pages=31–44|doi=10.2307/2384697|jstor=2384697|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
== Theories about the location == There have been many theories about the location of Takamagahara. Theories differ greatly depending on how the mythology in the Kojiki is interpreted.
=== 1. Celestial theory === According to the celestial theory, the gods must be in the heavens or the universe above the heavens since high heavens are the dwelling place of the gods.<ref name="Ishibashi 182"/><ref name=":3" /> This conceptual view is represented by [[:en:Motoori Norinaga|Norinaga Motoori]]'s theory; he believed it was disrespectful to gods and emperors to consider other theories.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Baskind|first1=James|url=https://brill.com/view/title/32221|title=The Myōtei Dialogues: A Japanese Christian Critique of Native Traditions|last2=Bowring|first2=Richard|date=2016-01-01|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-30729-2|doi=10.1163/9789004307292_005}}</ref> This idea was the mainstream view before [[World War II]] because of its strong connection with the emperor-centered [[:en:Historiography|Historiography]].<ref name=":1" />
=== 2. Terrestrial theory === The terrestrial theory suggests that mythology always contains some historical fact, and thus Takamagahara must also reflect what existed. This theory was first represented by [[Arai Hakuseki|Hakuseki Arai]], a [[:en:Confucianism|confucianist]] during middle of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. Specifically, he stated that Takamagahara was located in Taga County, Hitachi Province ([[:en:Hitachi Province|常陸国]]).<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":0" /> Also, some people believe Takamagahara existed, but outside of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]; one of the most popular such theories locates it at [[:en:Gangwon Province, South Korea|Gangwon]], [[South Korea]]. A chief proponent was the World War II war criminal, General [[:en:Kanji Ishiwara|Kanji Ishiwara]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Godart|first=G. Clinton|date=2015-11-02|title=Nichirenism, Utopianism, and Modernity: Rethinking Ishiwara Kanji's East Asia League Movement|journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|volume=42|issue=2|doi=10.18874/jjrs.42.2.2015.235-274|issn=0304-1042|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== 3. Kyushu-Yamatai-koku theory === The Kyushu-Yamatai-koku theory is that any of the candidate sites for the [[Yamatai|Yamatai-koku]] such as Yamamoto Country, Mii Country, Yamato Country, and Yasu Country in the [[:en:Chikugo River|Chikugo River]] basin.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Before the Nation|date=2003 |publisher=Duke University Press |isbn=978-0-8223-3183-4|pages=271–282|doi=10.1215/9780822384908-012}}</ref> Some people specifically believe that Mii Country is the Takamagahara and [[:en:Nakoku|Nakoku]] is the Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Nishitani |first=Tadashi|date=2010|title=Newest circumstances on Yamataikoku |url=http://joi.jlc.jst.go.jp/JST.JSTAGE/japt/75.277?from=CrossRef |journal=Journal of the Japanese Association for Petroleum Technology|volume=75|issue=4|pages=277–285|doi=10.3720/japt.75.277 |issn=1881-4131|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== 4. Artificiality theory === [[File:Nihonshoki tanaka version.jpg|thumb|A page from the ''Nihon Shoki'']]
The artificiality theory proposes that wondering about location of Takamagahara is meaningless since myths are made up. [[Yamagata Bantō|Banto Yamagata]], a scholar of Confucianism from the late Edo period, argues that the [[Age of the Gods|Jindai period]] (神代, Age of the Gods) in the ''Kojiki'' was a fiction created by later generations.<ref name=":4" /> A [[:en:Historian|Historian]] in 20th century, [[:ja:津田左右吉|Sokichi Tsuda]]'s view of history, which has become mainstream after the World War II, is based on his idea. Many scholars today also believe that the mythology of Takamagahara in ''Kojiki'' was created by the [[ruling class]] to make people believe that the class was precious because they originated in the heavenly realm.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Joos |first=Joël|date=2008-01-01|title=17. Memories Of A Liberal, Liberalism Of Memory: Tsuda Sōkichi And A Few Things He Forgot To Mention |url=https://brill.com/view/book/edcoll/9789004213203/Bej.9781905246380.i-382_018.xml|journal=The Power of Memory in Modern Japan |language=en|pages=291–307|doi=10.1163/ej.9781905246380.i-382.134 |isbn=9789004213203}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reader |first=Ian|date=2003|editor-last=Befu|editor-first=Harumi|editor2-last=Oguma|editor2-first=Eiji|title=Identity, Nihonjinron, and Academic (Dis)honesty|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=58 |issue=1|pages=103–116|jstor=3096753|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
== In Japan == [[File:Sangoku Meisho Zue Koyama Shijukusho Shrine.jpg|thumb|A drawing of a shrine from ''Sangoku Meisho Zue'']]
=== Takaharu-cho, Miyazaki Prefecture === The town of [[Takaharu, Miyazaki|Takaharu]], with Takachiho Mountain rising behind it, has long been recognized as the place of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]]'s descent. In the {{nihongo3||三国名勝図会|Sangoku Meisho Zue}}, a chronicle written by [[Satsuma Domain]] at the end of the Edo period, it is written that the name of this area, {{nihongo3||高原|Takaharu}}, is an abbreviation of {{nihongo3||高天原|Takamagahara}} and the area was the capital of Japan during ancient times.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Takaharu Cho Official Website |url=https://www.town.takaharu.lg.jp/soshiki/14/1270.html|access-date=2020-11-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原遥拝所 {{!}} 観光スポット {{!}} 高千穂町観光協会 {{!}} 宮崎県 高千穂の観光・宿泊・イベント情報|url=https://takachiho-kanko.info/sightseeing/detail.php?log=1338293391|access-date=2020-11-27|website=takachiho-kanko.info}}</ref> The chronicle also states that it is the reason why there are other local areas with similar names such as {{nihongo3||都島|Miyakojima}} and {{nihongo3||高城|Takajo}}.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kornicki|first1=P. F.|last2=Kracht |first2=Klaus|date=2001|title=Japanese Thought in the Tokugawa Era: A Bibliography of Western-Language Materials |journal=Monumenta Nipponica |volume=56|issue=3|pages=437 |doi=10.2307/3096806|jstor=3096806|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
As a proof of this record, {{nihongo3||天逆鉾|Amano-Sakahoko}}, the spear of gods, can be found at the top of the mountain. It is presumed that the spear was placed around the Edo period, but the details are still unknown.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Yamamoto |first=Hiroko|title=Chūsei shinwa |date=1998|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|isbn=4-00-430593-4|location=Tōkyō|oclc=41897511}}</ref> The town of Takaharu is also known as the birthplace of Emperor Jimmu. The main evidence is that Emperor Jimmu's infant name, "Sano-no-Mikoto", in the Nihon Shoki refers to the Sano area of the town.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lee|first=Peter H.|date=1978|title=''Die Religionen Koreas'' (review)|journal=Korean Studies|volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=193–199|doi=10.1353/ks.1978.0008 |s2cid=162289233|issn=1529-1529}}</ref> However, there is no detailed explanation about it, and the current description of Emperor Jimmu is largely based on {{nihongo3||三国名勝図絵|Sangoku Meisho Zue}}. According to the chronicle, Emperor Jimmu lived here until his [[:ja:神武東征|expedition to the east]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=神武天皇伝承地 {{!}} 高原町観光協会|url=http://www.takaharu-tourism.jp/look/jinmu/|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.takaharu-tourism.jp}}</ref>
=== Takachiho-cho, Miyazaki Prefecture === The town of [[Takachiho, Miyazaki|Takachiho]] is located at the Northern part of [[Miyazaki prefecture]]. Ama-no-Iwato, Mount Amanokagu, and Shiioji Peaks can be found in this area. [[Takachiho Shrine]] is known for its specific type of Shinto ritual ceremonial dance called Yoru-Kagura, which is said to have originated from a dance performed by Ame-no-Uzume.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高千穂町と日本神話|url=http://www.komisen.net/shinwa.htm|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.komisen.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=he Sacred Science of Ancient Japan: Lost Chronicles of the Age of the Gods|date=2014|publisher=Bear & Company}}</ref>
=== Soyo, Yamato-cho, Kumamoto Prefecture === Hinomiya-Heitate shrine, which calls itself the birthplace of the Takamagahara mythology, is at Soyo, [[:en:Kumamoto Prefecture|Kumamoto]]. Shintai, the sacred body of the kami, is a stone slab carved with two types of Jindai characters, and the characters "Asohi-no-okami (アソヒノオオミカミ)" and "Hifumi (日文)" are engraved on the front and back of the slab.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原（たかまがはら）日の宮・幣立（へいたて）神宮について |url=https://kumamoto.guide/look/terakoya/104.html|access-date=2020-11-27|website=【公式】熊本県観光サイト もっと、もーっと！くまもっと。 |language=ja}}</ref> The shrine's name "Heitate" means Himorogi, a sacred place or an altar, and it is said that this is the sacred place where the gods descended in ancient times.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Emoto|first=Masaru|title=Love thyself: the message from Water III|date=2004 |publisher=Hay House|isbn=1-4019-0899-3|location=Carlsbad, Calif.|oclc=60826467}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Harrison|first=Philomène |date=1970|title=The Indian Mind: Essentials of Indian Philosophy and Culture, and: The Chinese Mind: Essentials of Chinese Philosophy and Culture, and: The Japanese Mind: Essentials of Japanese Philosophy and Culture (review)|journal=Journal of the History of Philosophy|volume=8 |issue=1|pages=115–121|doi=10.1353/hph.2008.1620|s2cid=147200446 |issn=1538-4586}}</ref>
=== Takama, Gose-shi, Nara Prefecture === [[File:Mount Kongo(Kongosanchi)7.jpg|thumb|Mount Kongō viewed from [[:en:Mount Yamato Katsuragi|Mount Yamato Katsuragi]] ]] Takama is located on a plateau at the foot of Mount Kongo in [[:en:Gose, Nara|Gose-shi]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The region's old name is Katsuragi ({{nihongo2|葛城}}), and Mount Kongo was called Mount Takamagahara in ancient times.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天ヶ原 {{!}} 御所市 |url=https://www.city.gose.nara.jp/kankou/0000001484.html |access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.city.gose.nara.jp}}</ref> The Takamahiko Shrine is located at east side of Mount Kongo, and the area around the shrine is a traditional place where the gods of the heavens lived (Matsumura, 2014). The shrine is rated as the highest in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' ({{nihongo2|延喜式}}, ''Procedures of the Engi Era''), and its ''[[shintai]]'' ({{nihongo2|神体}}, body of the ''kami'') is a mountain located behind the shrine.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天彦神社 {{!}} 御所市|url=https://www.city.gose.nara.jp/kankou/0000001390.html|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.city.gose.nara.jp}}</ref> {{nihongo3||蜻蛉日記|[[:en:Kagerō Nikki|Kagero Nikki]]}}, a classical [[:en:Waka (poetry)|waka]], indicates that Amano-iwato was at [[:en:Mount Yamato Katsuragi|Mount Katsuragi]]. Since this poem was written around 974, it shows that this understanding dates back to at least the Heian period (794–1185).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hubbard |first1=Jamie|last2=Fu|first2=Charles Weihsun|last3=Heine |first3=Steven|date=1996|title=Japan in Traditional and Postmodern Perspectives|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=51|issue=1 |pages=130 |doi=10.2307/2385323|jstor=2385323|issn=0027-0741}}</ref> Similarly, {{nihongo3||三流抄|Sanryu-syo}}, the classical waka poem written in [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] (1185–1333), describes the location of Takamagahara as Mount Katsuragi.<ref>{{Cite book|author=Louis-Frédéric |title=Japan encyclopedia|date=2002 |publisher=Belknap Press of Harvard University Press|author2=Käthe Roth|isbn=0-674-00770-0 |location=Cambridge, Mass. |oclc=48943301}}</ref> Until the new Hitachi Province theory was proposed by Hakuseki Arai in the Edo period, this area was considered to be the location of Takamagahara. The stone monument of Takamagahara is in the parking lot of a temple in this area.<ref name=":4"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nishioka|first1=Hideo |last2=Schenck|first2=W. Egbert |date=January 1937|title=An Outline of Theories concerning the Prehistoric People of Japan|journal=American Anthropologist |volume=39|issue=1|pages=23–33|doi=10.1525/aa.1937.39.1.02a00030 |issn=0002-7294|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Iruzen, Maniwa City, Okayama Prefecture === Kayabe Shrine, Amano-Iwato, and Amano-Ukihashi are in the area of Hiruzen.<ref>{{Cite web|title=蒜山・高天原伝説｜真庭観光WEB |url=https://www.maniwa.or.jp/web/index.cgi?c=spot-2&pk=35|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.maniwa.or.jp|language=ja}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=神代遺蹟考|date=1928|publisher=松林堂書店}}</ref>
=== Oinuana, Ueno Village, Gunma Prefecture === The place was traditionally known as a small cave, but it was discovered to be much longer and deeper in 1929. The cave was named after what was believed to be the dwelling place of the Yamainu. Some places inside have been named as Takamagahara and Ama-no-Yasugawara.<ref>{{Cite book|title=上野村の文化財・芸能・伝説|date=2001|publisher=上野村教育委員会}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=郷土資料事典10|date=1997|publisher=ゼンリン}}</ref>
=== Taga County, Ibaraki Prefecture === According to the theory proposed by Hakusei Arai, kanji in ancient times were representing pronunciation of the Japanese language, and the original meaning of the [[:en:Kanji|Kanji]] does not match the meaning of the words they are describing. Therefore, the words expressed from them only explained [[:en:Pronunciation|Pronunciation]] not the actual meanings.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Metevelis|first=Peter |date=1994|title=Shinto Shrines or Shinto Temples?|journal=Asian Folklore Studies|volume=53|issue=2|pages=337–345 |doi=10.2307/1178650|jstor=1178650|issn=0385-2342}}</ref> In {{nihongo3||古史通|Koshitsu}}, Hakuseki interpreted Takamagahara in [[:en:Hiragana|Hiragana]] instead of kanji and compared it to Taga Country in Hitachi Province.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ohnuki-Tierney|first=Emiko|date=July 1991|title=The Emperor of Japan as Deity (Kami)|journal=Ethnology|volume=30|issue=3 |pages=199–215 |doi=10.2307/3773631|jstor=3773631|issn=0014-1828}}</ref> Also, he suggests that places called "Takaama-no-Ura” and "Takaama-no-Hara" in [[:en:Hitachi Province|Hitachi Province]] originated from Takamagahara.<ref name=":4"/><ref>{{Cite book|last=Levin|first=Judith|title=Japanese mythology |date=2008 |publisher=Rosen Central|isbn=978-1-4042-0736-3|edition=1st|location=New York|oclc=62533824}}</ref>
=== Iki, Nagasaki === The names of places such as "Amagahara (天ヶ原)" and "Takanohara (高野原)" still remain, and they are considered as "Heavenly Territory (天国領域)" according to the Kyushu-Yamatai-Koku theory.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Ushinawareta kyushu ocho.|date=February 1993|publisher=朝日新聞社 |author=Furuta, Takehiko|isbn=4-02-260750-5 |oclc=675223694}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Mizoguchi|first=Koji |chapter=Chapter 12 - Conclusion |title=The Archaeology of Japan |publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-03426-5 |location=New York |pages=326–334 |doi=10.1017/cbo9781139034265.015}}</ref>
== In South Korea ==
=== Goryeong County, North Gyeongsang Province === [[File:Gyeongsangbuk-do in South Korea.svg|thumb|Location of Gyeongsangbuk-do in South Korea]]
The Korean Peninsula theory was sometimes advocated mainly by amateur Korean researchers after World War II. Initially, [[:en:Chuncheon|Chuncheon City]] at [[:en:Gangwon Province, South Korea|Gangwon-do]] was considered to be the location of Takamagahara in South Korea because of certain lyrics from [[:en:Komagaku|Komagaku]], a type of traditional Japanese court music.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Seo Hyun-seop|year=2006|title=An analysis of conflicting viwepoints on historical issues in Japan-Korea relations|journal=県立長崎シーボルト大学国際情報学部紀要|volume=7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|author=Yao, Qiong|year=2015|title=Change and Changes to and Ways of Passing Down the Traditions of Ceremonial Rituals in ContemporarγJapanese Society －Focusing on Epidemic Elimination Ceremonial Rituals Originating with the SusanaδMyth|journal=NDLデジタルコレクション}}</ref>
However, in the 1990s, the chancellor of the Kaya University proposed a new theory called [[:en:Goryeong County|Goryeong County]] theory. He believes that the name of Mount Sori from Takamagahara mythology came from the capital city of South Korea, [[Seoul]], and therefore Goryeong County is its correct location. In 1999, a stone monument of Takamagahara (고천원고지비) was raised in [[Kaya University]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原|url=http://www.miraikoso.org/takaten/taka1.htm|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.miraikoso.org}}</ref>

{{For|the asteroid|10831 Takamagahara}}{{Jmyth infobox}}{{short description|Japanese mythological place}} In [[Japanese mythology]], {{nihongo|'''Takamagahara'''|高天原||"Plane of High [[:en:Heaven|Heaven]]" or "High Plane of Heaven"}}, also read as '''Takaamanohara''', '''Takamanohara''', '''Takaamagahara''', or '''Takaamahara''', is the abode of the heavenly gods (''[[amatsukami]]''). Often depicted as located up in the sky, it is believed to be connected to the Earth by the bridge ''[[Ame-no-ukihashi]]'' (the "Floating Bridge of Heaven").
== Overview == In [[Shinto]], ''ame'' ([[:en:Heaven|Heaven]]) is a lofty, sacred world, the home of the ''[[Kotoamatsukami]]''. Some scholars have attempted to explain the myth of descent of the gods from the Takamagahara as an allegory of the migration of peoples. However, it is likely to have referred from the beginning to a higher world in a religious sense. A Shinto myth explains that at the time of [[:en:Creation myth|creation]], light, pure elements branched off to become heaven (''[[:en:天|ame]]''). Heavy, turbid elements branched off to become earth (''[[:en:地|tsuchi]]''). ''Ame'' became the home of the ''amatsukami'' or gods of heaven, while ''tsuchi'' became the home of ''[[kunitsukami]]'' or gods of the land. The ''amatsukami'' are said to have descended from heaven to pacify and perfect this world.<ref>Basic Terms of Shinto'', Kokugakuin University, Tokyo 1985 p. 2.</ref>
== According to the ''Kojiki'' == In the beginning of the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (Records of Ancient Matters), Takamagahara is mentioned as the birthplace of the gods.<ref name="Ishibashi 182">{{Cite journal|last1=Ishibashi|first1=T. |last2=Dumoulin|first2=H.|date=January 1940|title=Yuiitsu-Shinto Myobo-Yoshu. Lehrabriss des Yuiitsu-Shinto|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=3|issue=1|pages=182|doi=10.2307/2382411 |jstor=2382411|issn=0027-0741}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Chaudhuri|first=Saroj Kumar |title=Hindu gods and goddesses in Japan|date=2003|publisher=Vedams eBooks (P) Ltd|isbn=81-7936-009-1 |location=New Delhi|oclc=54072517}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Stefan|last2=Brownlee |first2=John S.|last3=Mehl |first3=Margaret|date=1999 |title=Japanese Historians and the National Myths, 1600-1945: The Age of the Gods and Emperor Jinmu|journal=Journal of Japanese Studies|volume=25|issue=2|pages=406|doi=10.2307/133327 |jstor=133327|issn=0095-6848}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Matsunaga |first=Alicia Orloff|date=1966|title=The Land of Natural Affirmation. Pre-Buddhist Japan |journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=21|issue=1/2 |pages=203–209 |doi=10.2307/2383411 |jstor=2383411|issn=0027-0741}}</ref> It is assumed that Takamagahara existed in clouds above sea because there is a scene in which [[Kuniumi]] (国生み), the god of islands, lowers his spear to form an island. Also, when the goddess of the sun, [[Amaterasu]] (天照大御神) was born, she was commanded to rule Takamagahara by [[Izanagi]] (伊弉諾), the creator deity of creation and life.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|date=2006-04-01 |title=Nanzan guide to Japanese religions}}</ref><ref name="hdl.handle.net">{{Cite journal|title=天孫降臨説話と中臣・藤原氏 {{!}} 九大コレクション {{!}} 九州大学附属図書館|year=1971 |volume=103 |url=http://hdl.handle.net/2324/2236684 |language=ja |doi=10.15017/2236684|hdl=2324/2236684|last1=田村 |first1=圓澄 |journal=史淵 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=国生み {{!}} 神社本庁 |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/shinto/shinwa/story1|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.jinjahoncho.or.jp}}</ref> In the part related to [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] (スサノヲ, the brother of Amaterasu), Takamagahara is described as the place where many gods live with Ama-no-yasukawa (天の安河), Ama-no-iwato (天岩戸), paddy fields, and a place for weaving, giving an impression that life was close to the human world.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kirkland|first=Russell|title=Taoist Political Thought |journal=Encyclopedia of Political Theory|year=2010 |location=Thousand Oaks, CA |publisher=SAGE Publications, Inc.|doi=10.4135/9781412958660.n442|isbn=978-1-4129-5865-3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author=Sheets, William J. |year=2017 |title=Mythology in 21st Century Japan: A Study of Ame no Uzume no Mikoto|journal=OhioLINK}}</ref> It is stated that the [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]] (葦原の中つ国, the world between Heaven and Hell) was subjugated by the gods from Takamagahara, and the grandson of Amaterasu, [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] (瓊瓊杵尊), descended from Takamagahara to rule the area. From then on, the emperor, a descendant of Ninigi-no-Mikoto owned Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hardacre|first=Helen |title=Shinto: a history |year=2017|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1 |location=New York|publisher=Oxford University Press |oclc=947145263}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Isomae |first=Jun'ichi |date=2000-05-01 |title=Reappropriating the Japanese Myths: Motoori Norinaga and the Creation Myths of the Kojiki and Nihon shoki |journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|doi=10.18874/jjrs.27.1-2.2000.15-39 |issn=0304-1042|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[File:Origin_of_Iwato_Kagura_Dance_Amaterasu_by_Toyokuni_III_(Kunisada)_1856.png|thumb|Amaterasu, the Goddess of the [[sun]] and the universe.]] [[File:Kojiki Shinpukuji.jpg|thumb|A page from the Shinpukuji manuscript of the ''Kojiki'']]
== According to the other chronicles == In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' (日本書紀, ''The Chronicles of Japan''), there is almost no mention of Takamagahara in the text. It appears only in the fourth book of the first stage of {{nihongo3||神代記|Jindaiki}} and part of the [[:en:Posthumous name|Posthumous name]] which was given to [[:en:Empress Jitō|Empress Jito]] in the fourth year of [[Yōrō|Yoro era]] (720).<ref name="hdl.handle.net"/><ref name=":1"/><ref>{{Cite book |title=Imagining Exile in Heian Japan|date=2017-12-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-5497-3 |pages=17–42|doi=10.1515/9780824854973-003}}</ref>
In contrast, in the ''[[Fudoki]]'' (風土記, ancient reports on provincial culture and [[:en:Oral tradition|Oral tradition]]) written in [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] (710–794), the word Takamagahara appears only at the beginning of [[:ja:常陸国風土記|Hitachi-no-Kuni-Fudoki]] (常陸の国風土記).<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" />
Similarly, in the main text of ''[[Kogo Shūi|Kogo Shui]]'' (古語拾遺), a historical record written in the early [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (794–1185), Takamagahara is mentioned only in the section of Ninigi-no-Mikoto.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Naumann|first=Nelly|date=1982 |title="Sakahagi": The "Reverse Flaying" of the Heavenly Piebald Horse|journal=Asian Folklore Studies|volume=41|issue=1|pages=7–38 |doi=10.2307/1178306|jstor=1178306 |issn=0385-2342}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kanetomo|first=Yoshida|date=1992|title=Yuiitsu Shinto Myobo Yoshu|journal=Monumenta Nipponica |volume=47|issue=2 |pages=137–161|doi=10.2307/2385235|jstor=2385235|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
In modern times, Takamagahara was described as the "supreme celestial sphere" (至美天球) in ''Tales of the Spirit World'' ([[:ja:霊界物語|霊界物語]]) by [[:en:Onisaburo Deguchi|Onisaburo Deguchi]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Prophet Motive|date=2017-12-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0 |pages=20–44|doi=10.1515/9780824864040-003}}</ref> The "supreme celestial sphere" is illustrated as a spiritual world of pure light in the radiant universe.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Young|first=Richard Fox|date=1989|title=The Little-Lad Deity and the Dragon Princess. Jesus in a New World-Renewal Movement|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=44|issue=1|pages=31–44|doi=10.2307/2384697|jstor=2384697|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
== Theories about the location == There have been many theories about the location of Takamagahara. Theories differ greatly depending on how the mythology in the Kojiki is interpreted.
=== 1. Celestial theory === According to the celestial theory, the gods must be in the heavens or the universe above the heavens since high heavens are the dwelling place of the gods.<ref name="Ishibashi 182"/><ref name=":3" /> This conceptual view is represented by [[:en:Motoori Norinaga|Norinaga Motoori]]'s theory; he believed it was disrespectful to gods and emperors to consider other theories.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Baskind|first1=James|url=https://brill.com/view/title/32221|title=The Myōtei Dialogues: A Japanese Christian Critique of Native Traditions|last2=Bowring|first2=Richard|date=2016-01-01|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-30729-2|doi=10.1163/9789004307292_005}}</ref> This idea was the mainstream view before [[World War II]] because of its strong connection with the emperor-centered [[:en:Historiography|Historiography]].<ref name=":1" />
=== 2. Terrestrial theory === The terrestrial theory suggests that mythology always contains some historical fact, and thus Takamagahara must also reflect what existed. This theory was first represented by [[Arai Hakuseki|Hakuseki Arai]], a [[:en:Confucianism|confucianist]] during middle of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. Specifically, he stated that Takamagahara was located in Taga County, Hitachi Province ([[:en:Hitachi Province|常陸国]]).<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":0" /> Also, some people believe Takamagahara existed, but outside of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]; one of the most popular such theories locates it at [[:en:Gangwon Province, South Korea|Gangwon]], [[South Korea]]. A chief proponent was the World War II war criminal, General [[:en:Kanji Ishiwara|Kanji Ishiwara]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Godart|first=G. Clinton|date=2015-11-02|title=Nichirenism, Utopianism, and Modernity: Rethinking Ishiwara Kanji's East Asia League Movement|journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|volume=42|issue=2|doi=10.18874/jjrs.42.2.2015.235-274|issn=0304-1042|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== 3. Kyushu-Yamatai-koku theory === The Kyushu-Yamatai-koku theory is that any of the candidate sites for the [[Yamatai|Yamatai-koku]] such as Yamamoto Country, Mii Country, Yamato Country, and Yasu Country in the [[:en:Chikugo River|Chikugo River]] basin.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Before the Nation|date=2003 |publisher=Duke University Press |isbn=978-0-8223-3183-4|pages=271–282|doi=10.1215/9780822384908-012}}</ref> Some people specifically believe that Mii Country is the Takamagahara and [[:en:Nakoku|Nakoku]] is the Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Nishitani |first=Tadashi|date=2010|title=Newest circumstances on Yamataikoku |url=http://joi.jlc.jst.go.jp/JST.JSTAGE/japt/75.277?from=CrossRef |journal=Journal of the Japanese Association for Petroleum Technology|volume=75|issue=4|pages=277–285|doi=10.3720/japt.75.277 |issn=1881-4131|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== 4. Artificiality theory === [[File:Nihonshoki tanaka version.jpg|thumb|A page from the ''Nihon Shoki'']]
The artificiality theory proposes that wondering about location of Takamagahara is meaningless since myths are made up. [[Yamagata Bantō|Banto Yamagata]], a scholar of Confucianism from the late Edo period, argues that the [[Age of the Gods|Jindai period]] (神代, Age of the Gods) in the ''Kojiki'' was a fiction created by later generations.<ref name=":4" /> A [[:en:Historian|Historian]] in 20th century, [[:ja:津田左右吉|Sokichi Tsuda]]'s view of history, which has become mainstream after the World War II, is based on his idea. Many scholars today also believe that the mythology of Takamagahara in ''Kojiki'' was created by the [[ruling class]] to make people believe that the class was precious because they originated in the heavenly realm.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Joos |first=Joël|date=2008-01-01|title=17. Memories Of A Liberal, Liberalism Of Memory: Tsuda Sōkichi And A Few Things He Forgot To Mention |url=https://brill.com/view/book/edcoll/9789004213203/Bej.9781905246380.i-382_018.xml|journal=The Power of Memory in Modern Japan |language=en|pages=291–307|doi=10.1163/ej.9781905246380.i-382.134 |isbn=9789004213203}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reader |first=Ian|date=2003|editor-last=Befu|editor-first=Harumi|editor2-last=Oguma|editor2-first=Eiji|title=Identity, Nihonjinron, and Academic (Dis)honesty|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=58 |issue=1|pages=103–116|jstor=3096753|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
== In Japan == [[File:Sangoku Meisho Zue Koyama Shijukusho Shrine.jpg|thumb|A drawing of a shrine from ''Sangoku Meisho Zue'']]
=== Takaharu-cho, Miyazaki Prefecture === The town of [[Takaharu, Miyazaki|Takaharu]], with Takachiho Mountain rising behind it, has long been recognized as the place of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]]'s descent. In the {{nihongo3||三国名勝図会|Sangoku Meisho Zue}}, a chronicle written by [[Satsuma Domain]] at the end of the Edo period, it is written that the name of this area, {{nihongo3||高原|Takaharu}}, is an abbreviation of {{nihongo3||高天原|Takamagahara}} and the area was the capital of Japan during ancient times.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Takaharu Cho Official Website |url=https://www.town.takaharu.lg.jp/soshiki/14/1270.html|access-date=2020-11-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原遥拝所 {{!}} 観光スポット {{!}} 高千穂町観光協会 {{!}} 宮崎県 高千穂の観光・宿泊・イベント情報|url=https://takachiho-kanko.info/sightseeing/detail.php?log=1338293391|access-date=2020-11-27|website=takachiho-kanko.info}}</ref> The chronicle also states that it is the reason why there are other local areas with similar names such as {{nihongo3||都島|Miyakojima}} and {{nihongo3||高城|Takajo}}.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kornicki|first1=P. F.|last2=Kracht |first2=Klaus|date=2001|title=Japanese Thought in the Tokugawa Era: A Bibliography of Western-Language Materials |journal=Monumenta Nipponica |volume=56|issue=3|pages=437 |doi=10.2307/3096806|jstor=3096806|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
As a proof of this record, {{nihongo3||天逆鉾|Amano-Sakahoko}}, the spear of gods, can be found at the top of the mountain. It is presumed that the spear was placed around the Edo period, but the details are still unknown.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Yamamoto |first=Hiroko|title=Chūsei shinwa |date=1998|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|isbn=4-00-430593-4|location=Tōkyō|oclc=41897511}}</ref> The town of Takaharu is also known as the birthplace of Emperor Jimmu. The main evidence is that Emperor Jimmu's infant name, "Sano-no-Mikoto", in the Nihon Shoki refers to the Sano area of the town.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lee|first=Peter H.|date=1978|title=''Die Religionen Koreas'' (review)|journal=Korean Studies|volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=193–199|doi=10.1353/ks.1978.0008 |s2cid=162289233|issn=1529-1529}}</ref> However, there is no detailed explanation about it, and the current description of Emperor Jimmu is largely based on {{nihongo3||三国名勝図絵|Sangoku Meisho Zue}}. According to the chronicle, Emperor Jimmu lived here until his [[:ja:神武東征|expedition to the east]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=神武天皇伝承地 {{!}} 高原町観光協会|url=http://www.takaharu-tourism.jp/look/jinmu/|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.takaharu-tourism.jp}}</ref>
=== Takachiho-cho, Miyazaki Prefecture === The town of [[:en:Takachiho, Miyazaki|Takachiho]] is located at the Northern part of [[Miyazaki prefecture]]. Ama-no-Iwato, Mount Amanokagu, and Shiioji Peaks can be found in this area. [[Takachiho Shrine]] is known for its specific type of Shinto ritual ceremonial dance called Yoru-Kagura, which is said to have originated from a dance performed by Ame-no-Uzume.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高千穂町と日本神話|url=http://www.komisen.net/shinwa.htm|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.komisen.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=he Sacred Science of Ancient Japan: Lost Chronicles of the Age of the Gods|date=2014|publisher=Bear & Company}}</ref>
=== Soyo, Yamato-cho, Kumamoto Prefecture === Hinomiya-Heitate shrine, which calls itself the birthplace of the Takamagahara mythology, is at Soyo, [[:en:Kumamoto Prefecture|Kumamoto]]. Shintai, the sacred body of the kami, is a stone slab carved with two types of Jindai characters, and the characters "Asohi-no-okami (アソヒノオオミカミ)" and "Hifumi (日文)" are engraved on the front and back of the slab.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原（たかまがはら）日の宮・幣立（へいたて）神宮について |url=https://kumamoto.guide/look/terakoya/104.html|access-date=2020-11-27|website=【公式】熊本県観光サイト もっと、もーっと！くまもっと。 |language=ja}}</ref> The shrine's name "Heitate" means Himorogi, a sacred place or an altar, and it is said that this is the sacred place where the gods descended in ancient times.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Emoto|first=Masaru|title=Love thyself: the message from Water III|date=2004 |publisher=Hay House|isbn=1-4019-0899-3|location=Carlsbad, Calif.|oclc=60826467}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Harrison|first=Philomène |date=1970|title=The Indian Mind: Essentials of Indian Philosophy and Culture, and: The Chinese Mind: Essentials of Chinese Philosophy and Culture, and: The Japanese Mind: Essentials of Japanese Philosophy and Culture (review)|journal=Journal of the History of Philosophy|volume=8 |issue=1|pages=115–121|doi=10.1353/hph.2008.1620|s2cid=147200446 |issn=1538-4586}}</ref>
=== Takama, Gose-shi, Nara Prefecture === [[File:Mount Kongo(Kongosanchi)7.jpg|thumb|Mount Kongō viewed from [[:en:Mount Yamato Katsuragi|Mount Yamato Katsuragi]] ]] Takama is located on a plateau at the foot of Mount Kongo in [[:en:Gose, Nara|Gose-shi]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The region's old name is Katsuragi ({{nihongo2|葛城}}), and Mount Kongo was called Mount Takamagahara in ancient times.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天ヶ原 {{!}} 御所市 |url=https://www.city.gose.nara.jp/kankou/0000001484.html |access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.city.gose.nara.jp}}</ref> The Takamahiko Shrine is located at east side of Mount Kongo, and the area around the shrine is a traditional place where the gods of the heavens lived (Matsumura, 2014). The shrine is rated as the highest in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' ({{nihongo2|延喜式}}, ''Procedures of the Engi Era''), and its ''[[shintai]]'' ({{nihongo2|神体}}, body of the ''kami'') is a mountain located behind the shrine.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天彦神社 {{!}} 御所市|url=https://www.city.gose.nara.jp/kankou/0000001390.html|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.city.gose.nara.jp}}</ref> {{nihongo3||蜻蛉日記|[[:en:Kagerō Nikki|Kagero Nikki]]}}, a classical [[:en:Waka (poetry)|waka]], indicates that Amano-iwato was at [[:en:Mount Yamato Katsuragi|Mount Katsuragi]]. Since this poem was written around 974, it shows that this understanding dates back to at least the Heian period (794–1185).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hubbard |first1=Jamie|last2=Fu|first2=Charles Weihsun|last3=Heine |first3=Steven|date=1996|title=Japan in Traditional and Postmodern Perspectives|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=51|issue=1 |pages=130 |doi=10.2307/2385323|jstor=2385323|issn=0027-0741}}</ref> Similarly, {{nihongo3||三流抄|Sanryu-syo}}, the classical waka poem written in [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] (1185–1333), describes the location of Takamagahara as Mount Katsuragi.<ref>{{Cite book|author=Louis-Frédéric |title=Japan encyclopedia|date=2002 |publisher=Belknap Press of Harvard University Press|author2=Käthe Roth|isbn=0-674-00770-0 |location=Cambridge, Mass. |oclc=48943301}}</ref> Until the new Hitachi Province theory was proposed by Hakuseki Arai in the Edo period, this area was considered to be the location of Takamagahara. The stone monument of Takamagahara is in the parking lot of a temple in this area.<ref name=":4"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nishioka|first1=Hideo |last2=Schenck|first2=W. Egbert |date=January 1937|title=An Outline of Theories concerning the Prehistoric People of Japan|journal=American Anthropologist |volume=39|issue=1|pages=23–33|doi=10.1525/aa.1937.39.1.02a00030 |issn=0002-7294|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Iruzen, Maniwa City, Okayama Prefecture === Kayabe Shrine, Amano-Iwato, and Amano-Ukihashi are in the area of Hiruzen.<ref>{{Cite web|title=蒜山・高天原伝説｜真庭観光WEB |url=https://www.maniwa.or.jp/web/index.cgi?c=spot-2&pk=35|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.maniwa.or.jp|language=ja}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=神代遺蹟考|date=1928|publisher=松林堂書店}}</ref>
=== Oinuana, Ueno Village, Gunma Prefecture === The place was traditionally known as a small cave, but it was discovered to be much longer and deeper in 1929. The cave was named after what was believed to be the dwelling place of the Yamainu. Some places inside have been named as Takamagahara and Ama-no-Yasugawara.<ref>{{Cite book|title=上野村の文化財・芸能・伝説|date=2001|publisher=上野村教育委員会}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=郷土資料事典10|date=1997|publisher=ゼンリン}}</ref>
=== Taga County, Ibaraki Prefecture === According to the theory proposed by Hakusei Arai, kanji in ancient times were representing pronunciation of the Japanese language, and the original meaning of the [[:en:Kanji|Kanji]] does not match the meaning of the words they are describing. Therefore, the words expressed from them only explained [[:en:Pronunciation|Pronunciation]] not the actual meanings.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Metevelis|first=Peter |date=1994|title=Shinto Shrines or Shinto Temples?|journal=Asian Folklore Studies|volume=53|issue=2|pages=337–345 |doi=10.2307/1178650|jstor=1178650|issn=0385-2342}}</ref> In {{nihongo3||古史通|Koshitsu}}, Hakuseki interpreted Takamagahara in [[:en:Hiragana|Hiragana]] instead of kanji and compared it to Taga Country in Hitachi Province.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ohnuki-Tierney|first=Emiko|date=July 1991|title=The Emperor of Japan as Deity (Kami)|journal=Ethnology|volume=30|issue=3 |pages=199–215 |doi=10.2307/3773631|jstor=3773631|issn=0014-1828}}</ref> Also, he suggests that places called "Takaama-no-Ura” and "Takaama-no-Hara" in [[:en:Hitachi Province|Hitachi Province]] originated from Takamagahara.<ref name=":4"/><ref>{{Cite book|last=Levin|first=Judith|title=Japanese mythology |date=2008 |publisher=Rosen Central|isbn=978-1-4042-0736-3|edition=1st|location=New York|oclc=62533824}}</ref>
=== Iki, Nagasaki === The names of places such as "Amagahara (天ヶ原)" and "Takanohara (高野原)" still remain, and they are considered as "Heavenly Territory (天国領域)" according to the Kyushu-Yamatai-Koku theory.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Ushinawareta kyushu ocho.|date=February 1993|publisher=朝日新聞社 |author=Furuta, Takehiko|isbn=4-02-260750-5 |oclc=675223694}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Mizoguchi|first=Koji |chapter=Chapter 12 - Conclusion |title=The Archaeology of Japan |publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-03426-5 |location=New York |pages=326–334 |doi=10.1017/cbo9781139034265.015}}</ref>
== In South Korea ==
=== Goryeong County, North Gyeongsang Province === [[File:Gyeongsangbuk-do in South Korea.svg|thumb|Location of Gyeongsangbuk-do in South Korea]]
The Korean Peninsula theory was sometimes advocated mainly by amateur Korean researchers after World War II. Initially, [[:en:Chuncheon|Chuncheon City]] at [[:en:Gangwon Province, South Korea|Gangwon-do]] was considered to be the location of Takamagahara in South Korea because of certain lyrics from [[:en:Komagaku|Komagaku]], a type of traditional Japanese court music.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Seo Hyun-seop|year=2006|title=An analysis of conflicting viwepoints on historical issues in Japan-Korea relations|journal=県立長崎シーボルト大学国際情報学部紀要|volume=7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|author=Yao, Qiong|year=2015|title=Change and Changes to and Ways of Passing Down the Traditions of Ceremonial Rituals in ContemporarγJapanese Society －Focusing on Epidemic Elimination Ceremonial Rituals Originating with the SusanaδMyth|journal=NDLデジタルコレクション}}</ref>
However, in the 1990s, the chancellor of the Kaya University proposed a new theory called [[:en:Goryeong County|Goryeong County]] theory. He believes that the name of Mount Sori from Takamagahara mythology came from the capital city of South Korea, [[Seoul]], and therefore Goryeong County is its correct location. In 1999, a stone monument of Takamagahara (고천원고지비) was raised in [[Kaya University]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原|url=http://www.miraikoso.org/takaten/taka1.htm|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.miraikoso.org}}</ref>

{{For|the asteroid|10831 Takamagahara}}{{Jmyth infobox}}{{short description|Japanese mythological place}} In [[Japanese mythology]], {{nihongo|'''Takamagahara'''|高天原||"Plane of High [[:en:Heaven|Heaven]]" or "High Plane of Heaven"}}, also read as '''Takaamanohara''', '''Takamanohara''', '''Takaamagahara''', or '''Takaamahara''', is the abode of the heavenly gods (''[[amatsukami]]''). Often depicted as located up in the sky, it is believed to be connected to the Earth by the bridge ''[[Ame-no-ukihashi]]'' (the "Floating Bridge of Heaven").
== Overview == In [[Shinto]], ''ame'' ([[:en:Heaven|Heaven]]) is a lofty, sacred world, the home of the ''[[Kotoamatsukami]]''. Some scholars have attempted to explain the myth of descent of the gods from the Takamagahara as an allegory of the migration of peoples. However, it is likely to have referred from the beginning to a higher world in a religious sense. A Shinto myth explains that at the time of [[:en:Creation myth|creation]], light, pure elements branched off to become heaven (''[[:en:天|ame]]''). Heavy, turbid elements branched off to become earth (''[[:en:地|tsuchi]]''). ''Ame'' became the home of the ''amatsukami'' or gods of heaven, while ''tsuchi'' became the home of ''[[kunitsukami]]'' or gods of the land. The ''amatsukami'' are said to have descended from heaven to pacify and perfect this world.<ref>Basic Terms of Shinto'', Kokugakuin University, Tokyo 1985 p. 2.</ref>
== According to the ''Kojiki'' == In the beginning of the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (Records of Ancient Matters), Takamagahara is mentioned as the birthplace of the gods.<ref name="Ishibashi 182">{{Cite journal|last1=Ishibashi|first1=T. |last2=Dumoulin|first2=H.|date=January 1940|title=Yuiitsu-Shinto Myobo-Yoshu. Lehrabriss des Yuiitsu-Shinto|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=3|issue=1|pages=182|doi=10.2307/2382411 |jstor=2382411|issn=0027-0741}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Chaudhuri|first=Saroj Kumar |title=Hindu gods and goddesses in Japan|date=2003|publisher=Vedams eBooks (P) Ltd|isbn=81-7936-009-1 |location=New Delhi|oclc=54072517}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Stefan|last2=Brownlee |first2=John S.|last3=Mehl |first3=Margaret|date=1999 |title=Japanese Historians and the National Myths, 1600-1945: The Age of the Gods and Emperor Jinmu|journal=Journal of Japanese Studies|volume=25|issue=2|pages=406|doi=10.2307/133327 |jstor=133327|issn=0095-6848}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Matsunaga |first=Alicia Orloff|date=1966|title=The Land of Natural Affirmation. Pre-Buddhist Japan |journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=21|issue=1/2 |pages=203–209 |doi=10.2307/2383411 |jstor=2383411|issn=0027-0741}}</ref> It is assumed that Takamagahara existed in clouds above sea because there is a scene in which [[Kuniumi]] (国生み), the god of islands, lowers his spear to form an island. Also, when the goddess of the sun, [[Amaterasu]] (天照大御神) was born, she was commanded to rule Takamagahara by [[Izanagi]] (伊弉諾), the creator deity of creation and life.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|date=2006-04-01 |title=Nanzan guide to Japanese religions}}</ref><ref name="hdl.handle.net">{{Cite journal|title=天孫降臨説話と中臣・藤原氏 {{!}} 九大コレクション {{!}} 九州大学附属図書館|year=1971 |volume=103 |url=http://hdl.handle.net/2324/2236684 |language=ja |doi=10.15017/2236684|hdl=2324/2236684|last1=田村 |first1=圓澄 |journal=史淵 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=国生み {{!}} 神社本庁 |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/shinto/shinwa/story1|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.jinjahoncho.or.jp}}</ref> In the part related to [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] (スサノヲ, the brother of Amaterasu), Takamagahara is described as the place where many gods live with Ama-no-yasukawa (天の安河), Ama-no-iwato (天岩戸), paddy fields, and a place for weaving, giving an impression that life was close to the human world.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kirkland|first=Russell|title=Taoist Political Thought |journal=Encyclopedia of Political Theory|year=2010 |location=Thousand Oaks, CA |publisher=SAGE Publications, Inc.|doi=10.4135/9781412958660.n442|isbn=978-1-4129-5865-3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author=Sheets, William J. |year=2017 |title=Mythology in 21st Century Japan: A Study of Ame no Uzume no Mikoto|journal=OhioLINK}}</ref> It is stated that the [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni|Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]] (葦原の中つ国, the world between Heaven and Hell) was subjugated by the gods from Takamagahara, and the grandson of Amaterasu, [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] (瓊瓊杵尊), descended from Takamagahara to rule the area. From then on, the emperor, a descendant of Ninigi-no-Mikoto owned Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hardacre|first=Helen |title=Shinto: a history |year=2017|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1 |location=New York|publisher=Oxford University Press |oclc=947145263}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Isomae |first=Jun'ichi |date=2000-05-01 |title=Reappropriating the Japanese Myths: Motoori Norinaga and the Creation Myths of the Kojiki and Nihon shoki |journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|doi=10.18874/jjrs.27.1-2.2000.15-39 |issn=0304-1042|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[File:Origin_of_Iwato_Kagura_Dance_Amaterasu_by_Toyokuni_III_(Kunisada)_1856.png|thumb|Amaterasu, the Goddess of the [[sun]] and the universe.]] [[File:Kojiki Shinpukuji.jpg|thumb|A page from the Shinpukuji manuscript of the ''Kojiki'']]
== According to the other chronicles == In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' (日本書紀, ''The Chronicles of Japan''), there is almost no mention of Takamagahara in the text. It appears only in the fourth book of the first stage of {{nihongo3||神代記|Jindaiki}} and part of the [[:en:Posthumous name|Posthumous name]] which was given to [[:en:Empress Jitō|Empress Jito]] in the fourth year of [[Yōrō|Yoro era]] (720).<ref name="hdl.handle.net"/><ref name=":1"/><ref>{{Cite book |title=Imagining Exile in Heian Japan|date=2017-12-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-5497-3 |pages=17–42|doi=10.1515/9780824854973-003}}</ref>
In contrast, in the ''[[Fudoki]]'' (風土記, ancient reports on provincial culture and [[:en:Oral tradition|Oral tradition]]) written in [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] (710–794), the word Takamagahara appears only at the beginning of [[:ja:常陸国風土記|Hitachi-no-Kuni-Fudoki]] (常陸の国風土記).<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" />
Similarly, in the main text of ''[[Kogo Shūi|Kogo Shui]]'' (古語拾遺), a historical record written in the early [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (794–1185), Takamagahara is mentioned only in the section of Ninigi-no-Mikoto.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Naumann|first=Nelly|date=1982 |title="Sakahagi": The "Reverse Flaying" of the Heavenly Piebald Horse|journal=Asian Folklore Studies|volume=41|issue=1|pages=7–38 |doi=10.2307/1178306|jstor=1178306 |issn=0385-2342}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kanetomo|first=Yoshida|date=1992|title=Yuiitsu Shinto Myobo Yoshu|journal=Monumenta Nipponica |volume=47|issue=2 |pages=137–161|doi=10.2307/2385235|jstor=2385235|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
In modern times, Takamagahara was described as the "supreme celestial sphere" (至美天球) in ''Tales of the Spirit World'' ([[:ja:霊界物語|霊界物語]]) by [[:en:Onisaburo Deguchi|Onisaburo Deguchi]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Prophet Motive|date=2017-12-31|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6404-0 |pages=20–44|doi=10.1515/9780824864040-003}}</ref> The "supreme celestial sphere" is illustrated as a spiritual world of pure light in the radiant universe.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Young|first=Richard Fox|date=1989|title=The Little-Lad Deity and the Dragon Princess. Jesus in a New World-Renewal Movement|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=44|issue=1|pages=31–44|doi=10.2307/2384697|jstor=2384697|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
== Theories about the location == There have been many theories about the location of Takamagahara. Theories differ greatly depending on how the mythology in the Kojiki is interpreted.
=== 1. Celestial theory === According to the celestial theory, the gods must be in the heavens or the universe above the heavens since high heavens are the dwelling place of the gods.<ref name="Ishibashi 182"/><ref name=":3" /> This conceptual view is represented by [[:en:Motoori Norinaga|Norinaga Motoori]]'s theory; he believed it was disrespectful to gods and emperors to consider other theories.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Baskind|first1=James|url=https://brill.com/view/title/32221|title=The Myōtei Dialogues: A Japanese Christian Critique of Native Traditions|last2=Bowring|first2=Richard|date=2016-01-01|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-30729-2|doi=10.1163/9789004307292_005}}</ref> This idea was the mainstream view before [[World War II]] because of its strong connection with the emperor-centered [[:en:Historiography|Historiography]].<ref name=":1" />
=== 2. Terrestrial theory === The terrestrial theory suggests that mythology always contains some historical fact, and thus Takamagahara must also reflect what existed. This theory was first represented by [[Arai Hakuseki|Hakuseki Arai]], a [[:en:Confucianism|confucianist]] during middle of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. Specifically, he stated that Takamagahara was located in Taga County, Hitachi Province ([[:en:Hitachi Province|常陸国]]).<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":0" /> Also, some people believe Takamagahara existed, but outside of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]; one of the most popular such theories locates it at [[:en:Gangwon Province, South Korea|Gangwon]], [[South Korea]]. A chief proponent was the World War II war criminal, General [[:en:Kanji Ishiwara|Kanji Ishiwara]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Godart|first=G. Clinton|date=2015-11-02|title=Nichirenism, Utopianism, and Modernity: Rethinking Ishiwara Kanji's East Asia League Movement|journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies|volume=42|issue=2|doi=10.18874/jjrs.42.2.2015.235-274|issn=0304-1042|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== 3. Kyushu-Yamatai-koku theory === The Kyushu-Yamatai-koku theory is that any of the candidate sites for the [[Yamatai|Yamatai-koku]] such as Yamamoto Country, Mii Country, Yamato Country, and Yasu Country in the [[:en:Chikugo River|Chikugo River]] basin.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Before the Nation|date=2003 |publisher=Duke University Press |isbn=978-0-8223-3183-4|pages=271–282|doi=10.1215/9780822384908-012}}</ref> Some people specifically believe that Mii Country is the Takamagahara and [[:en:Nakoku|Nakoku]] is the Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Nishitani |first=Tadashi|date=2010|title=Newest circumstances on Yamataikoku |url=http://joi.jlc.jst.go.jp/JST.JSTAGE/japt/75.277?from=CrossRef |journal=Journal of the Japanese Association for Petroleum Technology|volume=75|issue=4|pages=277–285|doi=10.3720/japt.75.277 |issn=1881-4131|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== 4. Artificiality theory === [[File:Nihonshoki tanaka version.jpg|thumb|A page from the ''Nihon Shoki'']]
The artificiality theory proposes that wondering about location of Takamagahara is meaningless since myths are made up. [[Yamagata Bantō|Banto Yamagata]], a scholar of Confucianism from the late Edo period, argues that the [[Age of the Gods|Jindai period]] (神代, Age of the Gods) in the ''Kojiki'' was a fiction created by later generations.<ref name=":4" /> A [[:en:Historian|Historian]] in 20th century, [[:ja:津田左右吉|Sokichi Tsuda]]'s view of history, which has become mainstream after the World War II, is based on his idea. Many scholars today also believe that the mythology of Takamagahara in ''Kojiki'' was created by the [[ruling class]] to make people believe that the class was precious because they originated in the heavenly realm.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Joos |first=Joël|date=2008-01-01|title=17. Memories Of A Liberal, Liberalism Of Memory: Tsuda Sōkichi And A Few Things He Forgot To Mention |url=https://brill.com/view/book/edcoll/9789004213203/Bej.9781905246380.i-382_018.xml|journal=The Power of Memory in Modern Japan |language=en|pages=291–307|doi=10.1163/ej.9781905246380.i-382.134 |isbn=9789004213203}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reader |first=Ian|date=2003|editor-last=Befu|editor-first=Harumi|editor2-last=Oguma|editor2-first=Eiji|title=Identity, Nihonjinron, and Academic (Dis)honesty|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=58 |issue=1|pages=103–116|jstor=3096753|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
== In Japan == [[File:Sangoku Meisho Zue Koyama Shijukusho Shrine.jpg|thumb|A drawing of a shrine from ''Sangoku Meisho Zue'']]
=== Takaharu-cho, Miyazaki Prefecture === The town of [[:en:Takaharu, Miyazaki|Takaharu]], with Takachiho Mountain rising behind it, has long been recognized as the place of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]]'s descent. In the {{nihongo3||三国名勝図会|Sangoku Meisho Zue}}, a chronicle written by [[Satsuma Domain]] at the end of the Edo period, it is written that the name of this area, {{nihongo3||高原|Takaharu}}, is an abbreviation of {{nihongo3||高天原|Takamagahara}} and the area was the capital of Japan during ancient times.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Takaharu Cho Official Website |url=https://www.town.takaharu.lg.jp/soshiki/14/1270.html|access-date=2020-11-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原遥拝所 {{!}} 観光スポット {{!}} 高千穂町観光協会 {{!}} 宮崎県 高千穂の観光・宿泊・イベント情報|url=https://takachiho-kanko.info/sightseeing/detail.php?log=1338293391|access-date=2020-11-27|website=takachiho-kanko.info}}</ref> The chronicle also states that it is the reason why there are other local areas with similar names such as {{nihongo3||都島|Miyakojima}} and {{nihongo3||高城|Takajo}}.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kornicki|first1=P. F.|last2=Kracht |first2=Klaus|date=2001|title=Japanese Thought in the Tokugawa Era: A Bibliography of Western-Language Materials |journal=Monumenta Nipponica |volume=56|issue=3|pages=437 |doi=10.2307/3096806|jstor=3096806|issn=0027-0741}}</ref>
As a proof of this record, {{nihongo3||天逆鉾|Amano-Sakahoko}}, the spear of gods, can be found at the top of the mountain. It is presumed that the spear was placed around the Edo period, but the details are still unknown.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Yamamoto |first=Hiroko|title=Chūsei shinwa |date=1998|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|isbn=4-00-430593-4|location=Tōkyō|oclc=41897511}}</ref> The town of Takaharu is also known as the birthplace of Emperor Jimmu. The main evidence is that Emperor Jimmu's infant name, "Sano-no-Mikoto", in the Nihon Shoki refers to the Sano area of the town.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lee|first=Peter H.|date=1978|title=''Die Religionen Koreas'' (review)|journal=Korean Studies|volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=193–199|doi=10.1353/ks.1978.0008 |s2cid=162289233|issn=1529-1529}}</ref> However, there is no detailed explanation about it, and the current description of Emperor Jimmu is largely based on {{nihongo3||三国名勝図絵|Sangoku Meisho Zue}}. According to the chronicle, Emperor Jimmu lived here until his [[:ja:神武東征|expedition to the east]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=神武天皇伝承地 {{!}} 高原町観光協会|url=http://www.takaharu-tourism.jp/look/jinmu/|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.takaharu-tourism.jp}}</ref>
=== Takachiho-cho, Miyazaki Prefecture === The town of [[:en:Takachiho, Miyazaki|Takachiho]] is located at the Northern part of [[Miyazaki prefecture]]. Ama-no-Iwato, Mount Amanokagu, and Shiioji Peaks can be found in this area. [[Takachiho Shrine]] is known for its specific type of Shinto ritual ceremonial dance called Yoru-Kagura, which is said to have originated from a dance performed by Ame-no-Uzume.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高千穂町と日本神話|url=http://www.komisen.net/shinwa.htm|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.komisen.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=he Sacred Science of Ancient Japan: Lost Chronicles of the Age of the Gods|date=2014|publisher=Bear & Company}}</ref>
=== Soyo, Yamato-cho, Kumamoto Prefecture === Hinomiya-Heitate shrine, which calls itself the birthplace of the Takamagahara mythology, is at Soyo, [[:en:Kumamoto Prefecture|Kumamoto]]. Shintai, the sacred body of the kami, is a stone slab carved with two types of Jindai characters, and the characters "Asohi-no-okami (アソヒノオオミカミ)" and "Hifumi (日文)" are engraved on the front and back of the slab.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原（たかまがはら）日の宮・幣立（へいたて）神宮について |url=https://kumamoto.guide/look/terakoya/104.html|access-date=2020-11-27|website=【公式】熊本県観光サイト もっと、もーっと！くまもっと。 |language=ja}}</ref> The shrine's name "Heitate" means Himorogi, a sacred place or an altar, and it is said that this is the sacred place where the gods descended in ancient times.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Emoto|first=Masaru|title=Love thyself: the message from Water III|date=2004 |publisher=Hay House|isbn=1-4019-0899-3|location=Carlsbad, Calif.|oclc=60826467}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Harrison|first=Philomène |date=1970|title=The Indian Mind: Essentials of Indian Philosophy and Culture, and: The Chinese Mind: Essentials of Chinese Philosophy and Culture, and: The Japanese Mind: Essentials of Japanese Philosophy and Culture (review)|journal=Journal of the History of Philosophy|volume=8 |issue=1|pages=115–121|doi=10.1353/hph.2008.1620|s2cid=147200446 |issn=1538-4586}}</ref>
=== Takama, Gose-shi, Nara Prefecture === [[File:Mount Kongo(Kongosanchi)7.jpg|thumb|Mount Kongō viewed from [[:en:Mount Yamato Katsuragi|Mount Yamato Katsuragi]] ]] Takama is located on a plateau at the foot of Mount Kongo in [[:en:Gose, Nara|Gose-shi]], [[:en:Nara Prefecture|Nara Prefecture]]. The region's old name is Katsuragi ({{nihongo2|葛城}}), and Mount Kongo was called Mount Takamagahara in ancient times.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天ヶ原 {{!}} 御所市 |url=https://www.city.gose.nara.jp/kankou/0000001484.html |access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.city.gose.nara.jp}}</ref> The Takamahiko Shrine is located at east side of Mount Kongo, and the area around the shrine is a traditional place where the gods of the heavens lived (Matsumura, 2014). The shrine is rated as the highest in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' ({{nihongo2|延喜式}}, ''Procedures of the Engi Era''), and its ''[[shintai]]'' ({{nihongo2|神体}}, body of the ''kami'') is a mountain located behind the shrine.<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天彦神社 {{!}} 御所市|url=https://www.city.gose.nara.jp/kankou/0000001390.html|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.city.gose.nara.jp}}</ref> {{nihongo3||蜻蛉日記|[[:en:Kagerō Nikki|Kagero Nikki]]}}, a classical [[:en:Waka (poetry)|waka]], indicates that Amano-iwato was at [[:en:Mount Yamato Katsuragi|Mount Katsuragi]]. Since this poem was written around 974, it shows that this understanding dates back to at least the Heian period (794–1185).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hubbard |first1=Jamie|last2=Fu|first2=Charles Weihsun|last3=Heine |first3=Steven|date=1996|title=Japan in Traditional and Postmodern Perspectives|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=51|issue=1 |pages=130 |doi=10.2307/2385323|jstor=2385323|issn=0027-0741}}</ref> Similarly, {{nihongo3||三流抄|Sanryu-syo}}, the classical waka poem written in [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] (1185–1333), describes the location of Takamagahara as Mount Katsuragi.<ref>{{Cite book|author=Louis-Frédéric |title=Japan encyclopedia|date=2002 |publisher=Belknap Press of Harvard University Press|author2=Käthe Roth|isbn=0-674-00770-0 |location=Cambridge, Mass. |oclc=48943301}}</ref> Until the new Hitachi Province theory was proposed by Hakuseki Arai in the Edo period, this area was considered to be the location of Takamagahara. The stone monument of Takamagahara is in the parking lot of a temple in this area.<ref name=":4"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nishioka|first1=Hideo |last2=Schenck|first2=W. Egbert |date=January 1937|title=An Outline of Theories concerning the Prehistoric People of Japan|journal=American Anthropologist |volume=39|issue=1|pages=23–33|doi=10.1525/aa.1937.39.1.02a00030 |issn=0002-7294|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Iruzen, Maniwa City, Okayama Prefecture === Kayabe Shrine, Amano-Iwato, and Amano-Ukihashi are in the area of Hiruzen.<ref>{{Cite web|title=蒜山・高天原伝説｜真庭観光WEB |url=https://www.maniwa.or.jp/web/index.cgi?c=spot-2&pk=35|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.maniwa.or.jp|language=ja}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=神代遺蹟考|date=1928|publisher=松林堂書店}}</ref>
=== Oinuana, Ueno Village, Gunma Prefecture === The place was traditionally known as a small cave, but it was discovered to be much longer and deeper in 1929. The cave was named after what was believed to be the dwelling place of the Yamainu. Some places inside have been named as Takamagahara and Ama-no-Yasugawara.<ref>{{Cite book|title=上野村の文化財・芸能・伝説|date=2001|publisher=上野村教育委員会}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=郷土資料事典10|date=1997|publisher=ゼンリン}}</ref>
=== Taga County, Ibaraki Prefecture === According to the theory proposed by Hakusei Arai, kanji in ancient times were representing pronunciation of the Japanese language, and the original meaning of the [[:en:Kanji|Kanji]] does not match the meaning of the words they are describing. Therefore, the words expressed from them only explained [[:en:Pronunciation|Pronunciation]] not the actual meanings.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Metevelis|first=Peter |date=1994|title=Shinto Shrines or Shinto Temples?|journal=Asian Folklore Studies|volume=53|issue=2|pages=337–345 |doi=10.2307/1178650|jstor=1178650|issn=0385-2342}}</ref> In {{nihongo3||古史通|Koshitsu}}, Hakuseki interpreted Takamagahara in [[:en:Hiragana|Hiragana]] instead of kanji and compared it to Taga Country in Hitachi Province.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ohnuki-Tierney|first=Emiko|date=July 1991|title=The Emperor of Japan as Deity (Kami)|journal=Ethnology|volume=30|issue=3 |pages=199–215 |doi=10.2307/3773631|jstor=3773631|issn=0014-1828}}</ref> Also, he suggests that places called "Takaama-no-Ura” and "Takaama-no-Hara" in [[:en:Hitachi Province|Hitachi Province]] originated from Takamagahara.<ref name=":4"/><ref>{{Cite book|last=Levin|first=Judith|title=Japanese mythology |date=2008 |publisher=Rosen Central|isbn=978-1-4042-0736-3|edition=1st|location=New York|oclc=62533824}}</ref>
=== Iki, Nagasaki === The names of places such as "Amagahara (天ヶ原)" and "Takanohara (高野原)" still remain, and they are considered as "Heavenly Territory (天国領域)" according to the Kyushu-Yamatai-Koku theory.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Ushinawareta kyushu ocho.|date=February 1993|publisher=朝日新聞社 |author=Furuta, Takehiko|isbn=4-02-260750-5 |oclc=675223694}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Mizoguchi|first=Koji |chapter=Chapter 12 - Conclusion |title=The Archaeology of Japan |publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-03426-5 |location=New York |pages=326–334 |doi=10.1017/cbo9781139034265.015}}</ref>
== In South Korea ==
=== Goryeong County, North Gyeongsang Province === [[File:Gyeongsangbuk-do in South Korea.svg|thumb|Location of Gyeongsangbuk-do in South Korea]]
The Korean Peninsula theory was sometimes advocated mainly by amateur Korean researchers after World War II. Initially, [[:en:Chuncheon|Chuncheon City]] at [[:en:Gangwon Province, South Korea|Gangwon-do]] was considered to be the location of Takamagahara in South Korea because of certain lyrics from [[:en:Komagaku|Komagaku]], a type of traditional Japanese court music.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Seo Hyun-seop|year=2006|title=An analysis of conflicting viwepoints on historical issues in Japan-Korea relations|journal=県立長崎シーボルト大学国際情報学部紀要|volume=7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|author=Yao, Qiong|year=2015|title=Change and Changes to and Ways of Passing Down the Traditions of Ceremonial Rituals in ContemporarγJapanese Society －Focusing on Epidemic Elimination Ceremonial Rituals Originating with the SusanaδMyth|journal=NDLデジタルコレクション}}</ref>
However, in the 1990s, the chancellor of the Kaya University proposed a new theory called [[:en:Goryeong County|Goryeong County]] theory. He believes that the name of Mount Sori from Takamagahara mythology came from the capital city of South Korea, [[Seoul]], and therefore Goryeong County is its correct location. In 1999, a stone monument of Takamagahara (고천원고지비) was raised in [[Kaya University]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=高天原|url=http://www.miraikoso.org/takaten/taka1.htm|access-date=2020-11-27|website=www.miraikoso.org}}</ref>
